## **1. Installing and launching required R packages**

Before performing the analysis, the required R packages are loaded.\
These packages support data manipulation (tidyverse), statistical visualization (ggplot2, ggstatsplot), interactive graphics (plotly), scaling functions (scales), and correlation visualization (corrplot).

```{r}
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, ggstatsplot,ggplot2, plotly, scales,corrplot)
```

## **2. Loading the data**

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
data_cleaned <- read_csv("data/colombia_customers_processed.csv")
```

## **3. Distribution of Key Variables**

To understand the overall characteristics of the dataset, we first examine the distribution of key behavioral and engagement variables.

Some highly skewed variables, such as transaction volume and transaction counts, are log-transformed using log1p() to reduce skewness and improve visualization clarity.

The variables are then reshaped into long format using pivot_longer() so that multiple histograms can be displayed simultaneously using facet_wrap().

```{r}
data_cleaned %>%
  mutate(
    log_total_tx_volume = log1p(total_tx_volume),
    log_tx_count = log1p(tx_count),
    log_avg_tx_value = log1p(avg_tx_value)
  ) %>%
  select(
    churn_probability,
    customer_tenure,
    satisfaction_score,
    nps_score,
    support_tickets_count,
    active_products,
    log_total_tx_volume,
    log_tx_count,
    log_avg_tx_value
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "darkseagreen3", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal()
```

These histograms provide an overview of how key indicators are distributed across the dataset and help identify potential skewness, outliers, and variability among customers.

## **4. Correlation Analysis of Churn-Related Variables**

To examine the relationships between churn probability and customer behavior indicators, a correlation analysis is performed.

Only numerical variables that are relevant to customer engagement, transaction activity, and satisfaction are selected for the analysis.\
Spearman correlation is used because it is more robust to non-normal distributions and outliers compared with Pearson correlation.

```{r}
corr_df <- data_cleaned %>%
  select(
    churn_probability,
    total_tx_volume,
    tx_count,
    avg_tx_value,
    monthly_transaction_count,
    transaction_frequency,
    avg_daily_transactions,
    customer_tenure,
    satisfaction_score,
    nps_score,
    support_tickets_count,
    resolved_tickets_ratio,
    active_products,
    feature_usage_diversity,
    credit_utilization_ratio
  )

corr_mat <- cor(corr_df, use = "complete.obs", method = "spearman")

corrplot(
  corr_mat,
  method = "color",
  type = "upper",
  tl.col = "black",
  tl.cex = 0.7
)
```

The resulting correlation matrix provides a visual overview of the strength and direction of relationships between variables, helping to identify factors that may be associated with higher churn probability.

## **5. Supplementary Check: CLV Segment Profiling**

Customers are grouped according to their CLV (Customer Lifetime Value) segment to explore whether customer value tiers exhibit different behavioral patterns.

The summary statistics below calculate the average values of key engagement indicators within each CLV segment.

```{r}
profile_summary <- data_cleaned %>%
  group_by(clv_segment) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_clv = mean(customer_lifetime_value, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_tx_volume = mean(total_tx_volume, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_tx_count = mean(tx_count, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_products = mean(active_products, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_satisfaction = mean(satisfaction_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_churn = mean(churn_probability, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

profile_summary

profile_summary %>%
  pivot_longer(-clv_segment, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = clv_segment, y = value, fill = clv_segment)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The bar charts provide a comparative view of behavioral metrics across CLV segments, allowing analysts to observe how engagement, transaction activity, and churn probability differ between customer groups.

## **6. Churn Risk Analysis**

Next, we investigate how customer sentiment indicators relate to churn probability.

A scatter plot is constructed to examine the relationship between Net Promoter Score (NPS) and churn probability.\
A LOESS smoothing curve is added to highlight the overall trend between these variables.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5

p_nps <- ggplot(data_cleaned, aes(x = nps_score, y = churn_probability)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.15, width = 1, height = 0.01, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE, color = "darkred") +
  labs(
    title = "Churn Probability vs NPS Score",
    x = "NPS Score",
    y = "Churn Probability"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

p_nps


```

To further analyze customer sentiment effects, churn probability is compared across different satisfaction score levels.

A boxplot is used to visualize the distribution of churn probability for each satisfaction category.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5

p_satisfaction_box <- ggplot(
  data_cleaned,
  aes(
    x = factor(satisfaction_score, ordered = TRUE),
    y = churn_probability,
    fill = factor(satisfaction_score, ordered = TRUE)
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Churn Probability across Satisfaction Score Levels",
    x = "Satisfaction Score",
    y = "Churn Probability"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

p_satisfaction_box

```

The boxplot allows us to compare the variability and central tendency of churn probability across satisfaction levels.

## **7. Churn Probability by Number of Support Tickets**

Customer support interactions may reflect service issues or dissatisfaction.\
To examine this relationship, the average churn probability is calculated for each level of support ticket count.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

support_summary <- data_cleaned %>%
  group_by(support_tickets_count) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_churn = mean(churn_probability, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n()
  )

ggplot(support_summary, aes(x = support_tickets_count, y = avg_churn)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "darkred", size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.8, size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Churn Probability by Number of Support Tickets",
    x = "Number of Support Tickets",
    y = "Average Churn Probability"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

The line chart shows how churn risk changes as the number of support tickets increases, potentially indicating whether frequent support interactions are associated with higher churn probability.

## **8. Customer Tenure vs Churn**

Customer tenure is another important indicator of engagement.\
This visualization explores the relationship between the length of time a customer has been with the company and their churn probability.

```{r}

ggplot(
  data_cleaned,
  aes(
    x = customer_tenure,
    y = churn_probability
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.08, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE, color = "darkred") +
  labs(
    title = "Churn Probability by Customer Tenure",
    x = "Customer Tenure",
    y = "Churn Probability"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

The smoothing curve highlights the overall trend between customer tenure and churn probability across the dataset.

## **9. Active Products vs Churn**

Product adoption is often associated with customer loyalty.\
This analysis examines how the number of active products held by a customer relates to churn probability.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(
  data_cleaned,
  aes(
    x = factor(active_products),
    y = churn_probability,
    fill = factor(active_products)
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Churn Probability by Number of Active Products",
    x = "Number of Active Products",
    y = "Churn Probability"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The boxplot illustrates whether customers who hold more products tend to exhibit lower churn risk compared with customers with fewer active products.

## **10. Prototype Dashboard User Guide**

This section describes the design and usage of the prototype visual analytics dashboard developed using Shiny.\
The dashboard enables users to interactively explore customer churn patterns and behavioral indicators derived from the EDA analysis.

The prototype interface contains four main analytical modules:

-   Overview of customer indicators
-   Distribution analysis
-   Relationship exploration
-   Correlation analysis
-   Customer segment profiling

These modules allow users to examine churn risk from multiple perspectives and support exploratory investigation of customer behavior patterns.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## **10.1 Overview Dashboard**

![](images/clipboard-1668944365.png)

The **Overview page** provides a high-level summary of key customer indicators.

Key components include:

-   Total number of customers in the dataset
-   Average churn probability
-   Average number of active products
-   Average satisfaction score

These indicators allow users to quickly understand the overall customer profile and risk level before conducting deeper analysis.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## **10.2 Distribution Analysis**

![](images/clipboard-2861054610.png)

The **Distribution Analysis module** visualizes the distribution of important behavioral and engagement variables.

Users can explore variables such as:

-   transaction volume
-   transaction count
-   average transaction value
-   customer tenure
-   churn probability

Histograms allow analysts to identify skewness, outliers, and variability across the dataset.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## **10.3 Relationship Exploration**

![](images/clipboard-2610100679.png)

The **Relationship Exploration module** investigates how customer attributes relate to churn probability.

Examples of relationships visualized include:

-   churn probability vs NPS score
-   churn probability vs satisfaction score
-   churn probability vs number of active products
-   churn probability vs customer tenure

Scatter plots and boxplots help reveal potential behavioral patterns associated with higher churn risk.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## **10.4 Correlation Analysis**

![](images/clipboard-960189920.png)

The **Correlation Analysis module** displays a correlation matrix between churn probability and key behavioral indicators.

This module helps users identify which variables are strongly associated with churn risk, including:

-   transaction activity
-   satisfaction indicators
-   support interaction variables
-   engagement metrics

The correlation heatmap provides a quick overview of variable relationships across the dataset.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## **10.5 Customer Segment Profiling**

![](images/clipboard-2303684489.png)

The **Customer Segment Profiling module** summarizes behavioral patterns across CLV segments.

Customers are grouped into segments such as:

-   Bronze
-   Silver
-   Gold
-   Platinum

For each segment, the dashboard visualizes:

-   average churn probability
-   average transaction activity
-   average satisfaction score
-   number of active products

This analysis helps analysts understand how high-value customers differ from lower-value segments in terms of engagement and churn risk.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## **11. Summary**

The prototype dashboard integrates multiple exploratory modules to support churn risk analysis.

Through interactive visualizations, users can:

-   understand overall customer characteristics
-   explore variable distributions
-   analyze relationships between engagement indicators and churn
-   compare behavioral patterns across customer segments

These insights provide a foundation for further predictive modeling and the development of customer retention strategies.
